abstract: >-
  Most EEG source imaging methods assume brain activity arises from independent, focal sources and are validated mainly on their ability to localize a single generator, overlooking the brain's network structure and the co-activation of regions along it. We introduce weighted Connectome Spectrum Electromagnetic Tomography (wCSET), which replaces its predecessor CSET's L1 sparsity prior with a smooth, exponentially weighted L2 prior over the connectome-harmonic spectrum. We validate wCSET, CSET, three standard connectivity-agnostic methods, and a geometry-based (Laplace-Beltrami) alternative across three complementary studies that probe source reconstruction beyond localization. The first simulates activity propagating across a structural connectome, providing an exact network-level ground truth. The second uses a clinical cohort of 26 seizure-free patients with epilepsy, with the resected volume as ground truth. The third uses simultaneous scalp and intracranial EEG recordings, a rare direct electrophysiological benchmark. In simulation, wCSET matched standard methods at localizing a source's onset but substantially outperformed them at reconstructing the distributed co-activation patterns that follow as activity spreads, an advantage robust to noise and to considerable connectome corruption. The resection cohort reproduced this picture: wCSET's localization accuracy matched every other method. Against intracranial recordings, wCSET outperformed standard and connectivity-agnostic methods in one of two evaluable subjects and matched them in the other. A purely geometric alternative matched wCSET's own performance throughout, suggesting cortical geometry alone may capture much of what drives accurate distributed reconstruction. Together, these results establish wCSET as a principled step beyond localization-only source imaging, and introduce a validation framework for evaluating such methods against a source's full co-activation pattern rather than its location alone.

# Introduction {#sec-introduction}

Electroencephalography (EEG) offers unparalleled temporal resolution for studying neural dynamics _in vivo_, but scalp EEG recordings pay for it in spatial resolution [@nunez_electric_2006]. Source reconstruction recovers some of that lost precision through minimum norm estimates (MNE), which project the EEG signal onto a cortical surface modeled from the individual's own MRI [@hamalainen_interpreting_1994; @dale_improved_1993].

Three decades of variants followed, including sLORETA [@pascual-marqui_standardized_2002], eLORETA [@pascual-marqui_discrete_2007] and dSPM [@dale_dynamic_2000], but the goal barely changed: pinpoint the isolated region behind a signal, a practice known as source localization [@knosche_eegmeg_2022]. Connectivity approaches now treat the brain as an integrated network rather than a set of independent regions [@bressler_large-scale_2010], and localization-focused methods are increasingly out of step with that view.

This gap is technical, not just conceptual: these methods assume independent sources, a prior known to underperform one informed by the true source covariance [@wipf_unified_2009]. The off-diagonal terms of that covariance encode which regions are active together; ignoring them is defensible when activity is genuinely focal, but not once multiple regions are co-active. Others report that incorporating the source covariance also helps with leakage (or field spread), a well-known problem in EEG source reconstruction [@schoffelen_source_2009; @gonzalez-moreira_caulking_2018].

Several strategies try to close that gap. The earliest, smoothness priors such as LORETA [@pascual-marqui_low_1994] and LAURA [@grave_de_peralta_menendez_noninvasive_2001], already impose a non-diagonal source covariance, but one fixed by local geometry rather than informed by how regions actually interact. Functional priors from fMRI can constrain expected interactions [@liu_fmri-si-stbf_2021], though fMRI's hemodynamic response unfolds over seconds, too slow to meaningfully constrain millisecond-scale EEG dynamics. Data-driven approaches instead jointly estimate source activity and its covariance structure from the recordings themselves, at the cost of greater ill-posedness and computation (e.g., BC-VARETA [@gonzalez-moreira_third_2018]). A final strategy leans on structure–function coupling directly: since neural activity propagates along the brain's structural scaffolding, the connectome estimated from diffusion MRI tractography offers a principled, subject-specific prior instead [@ruequeralt_connectome_2024].

Graph Signal Processing (GSP) supplies the machinery for this coupling [@shuman_emerging_2013]. Eigendecomposing the connectome's graph Laplacian yields brain harmonics ordered by graph frequency: low frequencies capture smooth, globally integrated activity, high frequencies more locally segregated patterns [@shuman_emerging_2013; @atasoy_human_2016]. Each harmonic is a spatial pattern of co-activation across regions, so reconstructing activity in this basis amounts to reconstructing co-activation patterns. Projecting source activity onto this basis (the Graph Fourier Transform, @sec-connectome) yields a compact "connectome spectrum," since both fMRI and EEG source activity concentrate their energy in a handful of low-frequency harmonics [@rue-queralt_connectome_2021; @atasoy_human_2016]. Rué-Queralt et al. (2024) built on this: Connectome Spectrum Electromagnetic Tomography (CSET) enforces an L₁ sparsity prior in this spectrum, restricting solutions to a small number of active harmonics.

A parallel line of work asks whether geometry alone can do the job. Substituting the Beltrami-Laplace operator on the cortical mesh for the connectome's graph Laplacian trades long-range white-matter pathways for fine-grained local geometry [@pang_geometric_2023]. Wang et al. (2026) applied this idea to EEG/MEG source reconstruction with Geometric Basis Functions (GBF): whole-brain activity as a combination of the leading ~300 such eigenmodes under a logarithmically-decaying L₂ penalty [@wang_geometry_2026]. Siu et al. took a different route to the same source-reconstruction problem, using weighted Beltrami harmonics as a hard post-hoc spectral filter rather than a continuous penalty [@siu_structural_2026].

Unlike the geometry-based methods above, which weight low-order harmonics preferentially by construction, CSET does not weight its harmonics at all, which prevents it from separating biologically meaningful ones from noise-dominated ones. We close that gap with weighted CSET (wCSET): a weighted L₂ prior that decays exponentially with graph frequency, replacing CSET's L₁ prior with a continuous, eigenvalue-graded penalty in GBF's spirit, but applied to the connectome's graph Laplacian, retaining the white-matter awareness the geometry-based methods lack. The weighting is not arbitrary: Abdelnour et al. (2018) shows that functional connectivity's eigenvalues relate to the structural Laplacian's via an approximately exponential mapping, so a small number of low-frequency structural eigenmodes already dominate functional connectivity [@abdelnour_functional_2018].

Despite this progression toward increasingly principled spectral weightings, validation has not kept pace. Rué-Queralt et al. validated CSET by correlating reconstructed activity with fMRI from the same task, but fMRI's hemodynamic response reflects neural activity only indirectly and with substantial temporal blurring, making it a weak proxy for the electrophysiological ground truth these methods aim to reconstruct. Other works validate through source localization in epilepsy patients instead; even where source extent improves, the criterion is misaligned with what connectivity-informed methods are designed to capture: not a focal source's spatial footprint, but the co-activation patterns across interconnected networks, which localization accuracy does not measure.

The primary barrier to a more appropriate validation is that no single benchmark provides a complete ground truth for network-level co-activation: simulations are exact but idealized, resections are clinically grounded but spatially coarse, and intracranial recordings are direct but sparsely sampled. We therefore combine three complementary fronts (@fig-overview), evaluating CSET and wCSET on each:

- **Study I:** We simulate activity propagating across the structural connectome itself (@sec-data-synthetic), giving an exact, fully known ground truth for network-level co-activation that no empirical recording can offer. We test whether connectivity-informed methods reconstruct the co-activation patterns that follow a source's onset, and how robust they are to erroneous connectivity data.

- **Study II:** In a clinical epilepsy cohort, the resected epileptogenic zone serves as ground truth, with post-surgical success confirming it truly contained the source. We test whether connectivity-informed methods localize it as accurately as standard methods.

- **Study III:** We revive and extend Grova et al. (2016)'s framework [@grova_intracranial_2016; @afnan_assessing_2026] correlating MEG and intracranial EEG (iEEG), extending it to truly simultaneous EEG/iEEG recordings, the only electrophysiological ground truth free from neurovascular coupling, skull attenuation, and temporal blurring [@nunez_electric_2006]. Projecting EEG-reconstructed sources onto iEEG electrode locations allows direct comparison of reconstructed and recorded co-activation patterns, via spatial correlation computed at each time point.

Together, these studies form a multi-level validation framework that moves source imaging beyond localization as its sole benchmark.


# Materials and Methods

Three complementary studies validate wCSET (@fig-overview). All three reconstruct the EEG with the same pipeline and the same six methods: three standard connectivity-agnostic baselines (wMNE, dSPM, sLORETA), two connectivity-informed methods (CSET, wCSET), and one geometry-based method (GBF). This section therefore first describes the shared pipeline (@sec-pipeline), then the datasets with their study-specific settings (@sec-datasets), and finally the metrics that compare the reconstructions with each study's ground truth (@sec-metrics).

![**Source reconstruction pipeline and the three validation studies.** All studies share one pipeline (top): MRI and electrode positions define the source space and forward model, the structural connectome provides the graph harmonics, and six inverse methods yield a reconstructed activity map. Red denotes brain activity and green denotes ground truth. **Study I (left):** activity is simulated as spreading across the structural connectome from a focal source, and the averaged EEG is reconstructed. Each method's map is compared with the ground truth by spatial correlation at each time point, shown for a single example at onset (t₁) and after spread (t₂) for wCSET and sLORETA only (the same example is shown in more detail in @sec-s1-localization); localization of the onset is evaluated separately (@sec-metric-loc). **Study II (middle):** in patients who were seizure-free after surgery, the location of maximal reconstructed activity is compared with the resection volume, measured as the Euclidean distance (0 mm if inside). **Study III (right):** EEG-reconstructed sources are projected onto the iEEG electrode positions ("virtual iEEG") and compared with the recorded iEEG (ground truth) by polarity-invariant spatial correlation across channels at each time point.](results/overview_method.png){#fig-overview fig-alt="Schematic of the shared source reconstruction pipeline (MRI and electrode positions, source space, forward model, connectome and harmonics, inverse solution, reconstructed activity) branching into three study panels: simulation with ground-truth and reconstructed brain maps at two time points, resection cohort with the distance between estimated location and resection volume, and simultaneous EEG/iEEG with reconstructed sources projected onto intracranial electrodes."}

## Source Reconstruction Pipeline {#sec-pipeline}

### Source Space {#sec-source-space}

Neural activity was modeled using a distributed dipole model with a cortical constraint: the source space restricted to the cortical white matter surface, reconstructed from T1-weighted MRI using FreeSurfer (v.7.4.1), with 7,275–7,653 dipoles uniformly distributed across it via MNE-Python [@gramfort_meg_2013] at ~3.3 mm average spacing, orientations fixed normal to the cortical manifold (full subdivision scheme, tool versions, and orientation-constraint rationale in Annex).

### Volume Conduction Model {#sec-bem}

Volume conduction was modeled with a Boundary Element Model (BEM) [@hamalainen_realistic_1989] using MNE-Python's default conductivities (0.3 S/m brain/scalp, 0.006 S/m skull). We built the head model with a custom SimNIBS CHARM-based pipeline [@puonti_accurate_2020], fitting inner skull, outer skull, and scalp surfaces sequentially and non-intersecting (full pipeline and BEM comparison in Annex). In the clinical studies, EEG sensors were pre-co-registered to the T1-weighted MRI and thus intrinsically aligned with the head model; in the simulation, the template EEG montage was projected onto the skin surface of the BEM. The forward solution (gain matrix) was computed via MNE-Python.

### Connectivity Matrices {#sec-connectome}

The brain is modeled as a graph (connectome) whose nodes are the source-space dipoles and whose edges represent physical anatomical links between them. The empirical connectome is available only for Study I's VEPCON subject; Studies II and III, lacking diffusion MRI, use the atlas surrogate below (@sec-data-resection, @sec-data-ieeg).

**Empirical connectomes**

Two types of structural links are incorporated: long-range connections from dMRI tractography, and short-range connections linking each dipole to its geodesically nearest neighbors, capturing local gray matter connectivity missed by standard tractography (thresholds in Annex); edges are weighted by distance — fiber length for long-range, geodesic distance for local.

**Connectome surrogates**

Where diffusion data is unavailable, we evaluate three connectome surrogates, validated via our simulation framework (@sec-study1) and summarized in @tbl-surrogates; two are also tested in binarized form (edge presence only) to isolate topology from edge-weight fidelity, yielding five variants in total. The atlas surrogate relies on the multi-scale connectivity (MultiConn) atlas [@aleman-gomez_multi-scale_2022], a probabilistic population atlas of the human structural connectome, used at scale 4.

| Surrogate | Construction | Binarized variant? | Tests whether... |
|:---|:---|:---:|:---|
| Atlas | Long-range tracts from the MultiConn atlas's [@aleman-gomez_multi-scale_2022] reference population, plus gray matter connections as above (Annex) | Yes | A population atlas can substitute for subject-specific tractography |
| Local | Gray matter connectivity only, plus homotopic cross-hemisphere links to keep the graph connected (Annex) | Yes | Local geometry alone, without long-range information, suffices |
| Beltrami-operator | Laplace-Beltrami eigenmodes of the cortical mesh directly [@pang_geometric_2023] — no explicit connectome graph is built (Annex) | No — purest geometry-only control | Cortical geometry alone suffices |

: Connectome surrogates. {#tbl-surrogates}

**Graph Fourier Transform**

Edge weights are distances, so we invert them to obtain an adjacency matrix $\mathbf A$ that describes connection strength. This is consistent with the approximately exponential decay of connectivity strength with distance [@ercsey-ravasz_predictive_2013]: shorter, more direct connections couple more strongly. From $\mathbf A$, we build the normalized graph Laplacian $\mathcal L = \mathbf I - \mathbf D^{-1/2}\mathbf A\mathbf D^{-1/2}$, where $\mathbf D$ is the degree matrix, the operator underlying Graph Signal Processing (GSP) on neural data [@shuman_emerging_2013; @ortega_graph_2018].

The eigendecomposition of $\mathcal L$ defines the Graph Fourier Transform (GFT):

$$
\mathcal L = \mathbf{U}\mathbf{\Lambda}\mathbf{U}^\top
$$

Here the columns of $\mathbf{U} = [u_1, u_2, \ldots, u_N]$ are the eigenvectors of $\mathcal L$, which we call graph harmonics, and $\mathbf{\Lambda}$ contains the corresponding eigenvalues, their graph frequencies. The GFT expresses brain activity in this harmonic basis. For GBF, the Laplace-Beltrami operator of the cortical mesh replaces $\mathcal L$, and its eigenmodes replace $\mathbf U$.

### Inverse Problem and Methods {#sec-inverse}

Every study used MNE-Python's wMNE [@hamalainen_interpreting_1994], dSPM [@dale_dynamic_2000], and sLORETA [@pascual-marqui_standardized_2002] as standard baselines against two connectivity-informed methods, CSET and wCSET, and one geometry-based method, GBF. All methods were whitened using an empirically estimated noise covariance [@dale_dynamic_2000; @knosche_eegmeg_2022] (exception: Study II, see @sec-data-resection).

**General formulation.** We estimate dipole activities $\mathbf s\in \mathbb R^n$ from sensor measurements $\mathbf y \in \mathbb R^m$ via the forward model $\mathbf y = \mathbf L \mathbf s + \epsilon$, where $\mathbf L$ is the lead-field matrix; because $n\gg m$, the problem is ill-posed. The Maximum A Posteriori (MAP) estimate is the regularized least-squares problem:

$$
\mathbf s^* = \text{arg }\underset{\mathbf s}{\text{min}}\underbrace{\lVert\mathbf y-\mathbf L\mathbf s\rVert_2^2}_{\text{Data Fidelity}} + \lambda\underbrace{\lVert \mathbf C \mathbf s\rVert_p^p}_{\text{Regularization}} \tag{1}
$$

Here $\lambda$ balances data fit against the prior (@sec-lambda), and $\mathbf C$ encodes the prior. For $p=2$, the prior is Gaussian with source covariance $\mathbf\Sigma_{\mathbf s}=(\mathbf C^\top\mathbf C)^{-1}$.

**Solvers.** For $p=1$, the solution is sparse; it has no closed form and is solved via proximal gradient descent. For $p=2$, the solution is analytic. Writing $\mathbf\Sigma_{\mathbf s}=\mathbf B\mathbf B^\top$ and decomposing $\mathbf L\mathbf B=\mathbf E_f\mathbf\Gamma\mathbf E_\ell^\top$ by singular value decomposition (singular values $\gamma_k$), it is computed as in MNE-Python [@gramfort_meg_2013]:

$$
\mathbf s^*=\mathbf B\,\mathbf E_\ell\,\mathbf D_\lambda\,\mathbf E_f^\top\mathbf y,\qquad \mathbf D_\lambda=\mathrm{diag}\!\left(\frac{\gamma_k}{\gamma_k^2+\lambda}\right) \tag{2}
$$

**Connectivity-agnostic priors.** sLORETA and dSPM use $\mathbf C=\mathbf I$ and $p=2$, then standardize the solution post hoc (Annex). wMNE uses $p=2$ and $\mathbf C=\mathbf W_d^{-1}$, where the depth-weighting matrix $W_{d,ii}=\lVert\mathbf L_{:i}\rVert^{-\kappa}$ ($\kappa=0.8$) counteracts the bias toward superficial dipoles. In all three, $\mathbf C$, and hence $\mathbf\Sigma_{\mathbf s}$, is diagonal: every pair of sources is uncorrelated a priori, and depth weighting only changes their variances. Nothing in the prior encodes which regions co-activate, which is why we call these methods connectivity-agnostic.

**Connectivity-informed priors.** CSET and wCSET penalize the depth-weighted source activity in the connectome spectrum, $\mathbf U^\top\mathbf W_d^{-1}\mathbf s$ ($\kappa=0.2$, tuned in simulation, @sec-study1). $\mathbf C$ is then no longer diagonal: the connectome harmonics couple the sources. Since the connectome spectrum is compact, CSET [@ruequeralt_connectome_2024] uses a sparse prior ($p=1$):

$$
\mathbf s^* = \text{arg }\underset{\mathbf s}{\text{min}}\lVert\mathbf y-\mathbf L\mathbf s\rVert_2^2 + \lambda\lVert \mathbf U^\top\mathbf W_d^{-1}\mathbf s\rVert_1 \tag{3}
$$

wCSET adds harmonic weights that follow an exponential low-pass filter on graph frequency, $W_{h,ii} = \exp(-\beta\lambda_i)$ ($\lambda_i$: eigenvalue of harmonic $i$, in $[0, 2]$; $\beta = 5$, tuned in simulation), and uses a smooth prior ($p=2$):

$$
\mathbf s^* = \text{arg }\underset{\mathbf s}{\text{min}}\lVert\mathbf y-\mathbf L\mathbf s\rVert_2^2 + \lambda\lVert \mathbf W_h^{-1}\mathbf U^\top\mathbf W_d^{-1}\mathbf s\rVert_2^2 \tag{4}
$$

High graph frequencies are thus penalized most, and $\mathbf\Sigma_{\mathbf s}=\mathbf W_d\mathbf U\mathbf W_h^2\mathbf U^\top\mathbf W_d$. The solution is Eq. (2) with $\mathbf B=\mathbf W_d\mathbf U\mathbf W_h$.

**Geometry-based prior.** GBF [@wang_geometry_2026] is implemented as wCSET with three substitutions: the Laplace-Beltrami eigenmodes of the cortical mesh $\mathbf U_{\text{LB}}$ replace $\mathbf U$ (@sec-connectome), $\mathbf W_d=\mathbf I$, and $\mathbf W_h$ becomes GBF's hard-truncated, log-form weighting (cutoff $S=150$; formula and tuning in Annex). Its solution is Eq. (2) with $\mathbf B=\mathbf U_{\text{LB}}\mathbf W_h$. It was tested in all three studies: as the Beltrami connectome surrogate in Study I (@sec-s1-surrogates), and alongside the other methods in Studies II and III (@sec-study2, @sec-study3).

### Regularization Parameter Selection {#sec-lambda}

For all methods except CSET, $\lambda$ is set per run from the evoked response's own estimated peak-amplitude SNR rather than fixed a priori, following MNE-Python's convention $\lambda = 1/\text{SNR}^2$, floored at $\lambda = \max(0.01, 1/\text{SNR}^2)$ so regularization doesn't vanish at high SNR. CSET is the exception: its $\lambda$ is instead fixed at $0.1$, tuned once against reconstruction accuracy in simulation (@sec-study1) rather than re-estimated per run.

## Datasets and Study-Specific Settings {#sec-datasets}

### Synthetic Data {#sec-data-synthetic}

Simulations used anatomical data from a single representative VEPCON subject [@pascucci_source_2022] (T1-weighted MRI and DTI tractogram), with EEG simulated on the 204-channel montage used throughout (@sec-data-resection). The cortical source space (@sec-source-space) was parcellated into 446 regions, using the same cortical parcellation as scale 4 of the MultiConn atlas (@sec-connectome). From these, 100 regions were selected via farthest-point sampling as a spatially uniform probe set, reused throughout except for the noise-robustness analysis (@sec-s1-data-noise), which instead uses a separate, independently sampled 50-region subset (kept smaller since it sweeps multiple SNR levels per region).

In each trial, a source region drawn from the probe set was assigned a 50 ms double-Hanning-window spike waveform [@dewouters_source-reconstructed_2026] (mimicking a clinical interictal spike) on all its dipoles. This follows approaches modelling epileptiform activity as a patch of simultaneously active dipoles rather than a point source [@afnan_eegmeg_2024]. The spike repeated every 1 s across a 20 s recording; after propagation and sensor projection (below and @sec-bem), the 20 resulting events were epoched and averaged into a single evoked response per run.

**Propagation model.** Activity was propagated across the connectome in a feedforward manner, with each dipole's activity a delayed and spatially-decayed copy of the source waveform:

$$
S_j(t) = \gamma^{h_j} \cdot s_0\!\left(t - \tau_j\right)
$$

where $h_j$ is the hop count from source to dipole $j$, $\gamma = 0.5$ is a per-hop spatial decay factor, and $\tau_j$ is a propagation delay based on conduction speed, nodal delay, and timing jitter (full model in Annex).

**Noise model.** Pink noise (source level) and white noise (sensor level) were calibrated to a literature-typical 15 µV RMS baseline [@nunez_electric_2006] and a single-trial SNR of 5 (parameter values in Annex Table 1; derivation also in the Annex).

Each simulation was repeated 8 times per source region; region/repetition counts were set via a power analysis for the region-paired comparisons reported in Results (full analysis in Annex).

**Inverse crime.** For Study I only, a second forward solution used a deliberately mismatched skull conductivity (0.012 S/m, brain/scalp unchanged) to avoid the inverse crime [@wirgin_inverse_2004] — the circularity of using the same head model to both generate and invert simulated data, which inflates apparent accuracy (precedent in Annex); the two models differ by approximately 10% (Annex).

**Connectome perturbation.** To test robustness to imperfect connectome knowledge, we perturb the connectome before source reconstruction (@sec-s1-prior-noise) via a degree-preserving double-edge swap (two random edges re-paired, degree unchanged), at severities from 0–100% of total edges.

**Preprocessing.** The epochs were processed with a Common Average Reference [@bertrand_theoretical_1985], baseline correction, and noise-covariance estimation from the pre-spike period before averaging.

### Clinical Dataset A — Resection Cohort {#sec-data-resection}

We used the dataset of @vorderwulbecke_high-density_2025 to validate EEG source imaging clinically: 44 patients with pharmacoresistant focal epilepsy who underwent resective surgery, outcome graded on the ILAE scale at 12 months (1 = seizure-free, 2–6 = increasing persistent seizures). We restricted analysis to seizure-free outcomes (ILAE 1, 28 patients) — for residual-seizure patients, the resection may not fully encompass the true epileptogenic zone, an unreliable ground truth — and excluded two more (no genuine resection cavity; missing EEG channel locations for coregistration), leaving 26 patients. Each had a pre- and post-operative T1-weighted MRI and a pre-operative interictal EEG recording (resection masks described below); epileptic spikes had been visually identified by clinical experts among the dataset's authors and time-locked averaged at their peak. The dataset's 257-channel EEG (HydroCel Geodesic Sensor Net) was reduced to the 204-channel montage used throughout by excluding cheek electrodes. As individual diffusion MRI was unavailable, the structural connectome was instead derived from the population probabilistic tractography atlas (@sec-connectome).

**Preprocessing.** EEG arrived as pre-averaged spikes, already filtered, downsampled, and interpolated by the data providers (@vorderwulbecke_high-density_2025; parameters in Annex); without individual epochs, noise-covariance estimation was not possible and an ad-hoc identity covariance was used instead (no whitening). A Common Average Reference, a notch filter for residual 50 Hz noise, and baseline correction were applied where needed.

**Ground truth.** Ground-truth brain activity maps are not directly available clinically, so we use the resected area, since these patients were seizure-free after surgery, marking their resection as containing the epileptogenic zone.

**Resection mask segmentation.** Resection masks were generated with RAMPS [@simpson_automated_2025], which estimates resected volume from pre-/post-operative T1-weighted MRI along with the resection's hemisphere and lobe (determined from clinical records or visual comparison; Annex). Masks were then visually inspected for quality (by overlaying pre-/post-operative T1w and mask), with manual segmentation used to replace unusable automated masks. Subjects whose mask remained missing, incomplete, or incorrect after this process were excluded (see above).

### Clinical Dataset B — Simultaneous EEG/iEEG Cohort {#sec-data-ieeg}

To validate source reconstruction against ground-truth intracranial activity, we used a cohort of 4 patients with simultaneously recorded scalp EEG and intracranial EEG (iEEG).

Epileptic spikes were identified and epoched in both modalities, time-locked to the same events, yielding paired scalp/intracranial recordings of the same underlying activity. Spikes were visually identified and marked on iEEG, cross-validated using Delphos, an automated spike detector [@roehri_time-frequency_2016; @roehri_assets_2017], following the same acquisition and marking protocol used for this cohort by @roehri_scalp-negative_2025. Each patient's pre-operative T1-weighted MRI was processed identically to the resection cohort (Clinical Dataset A) for anatomical/forward modeling (@sec-pipeline), and the structural connectome was derived the same way (individual diffusion MRI was likewise unavailable). Results are reported in the main text for the two subjects with a visible scalp EEG spike; the other two had deep sources with no visible spike, making their EEG-derived reconstruction — and the virtual iEEG projected from it (@sec-virtual-ieeg) — inherently unreliable, so their results appear in the Annex instead.

**Preprocessing.** EEG epochs were processed as in Study I (Common Average Reference, baseline correction, and noise-covariance estimation from the pre-spike period) and averaged into the evoked response: 130–265 marked spikes per subject.

**Ground truth.** iEEG epochs were averaged directly into the ground-truth evoked response, with no further preprocessing. Intracranial recordings provide ground-truth potential only at sparse electrode locations; reconstructed dipole-current maps are therefore projected onto these locations via a simplified forward model (@sec-virtual-ieeg) for direct comparison.

## Performance Evaluation Metrics {#sec-metrics}

### Map to map comparison {#sec-metric-corr}

Each method is evaluated via the (signed) Pearson spatial correlation between reconstructed and ground-truth activity maps at each time point:
$$
\mathcal{C}(t) = \frac{\sum_i \mathbf{s}^t_{\text{true}}(i) \cdot \mathbf{s}^t_{\text{est}}(i)}{\sigma_{\text{true}}(t) \cdot \sigma_{\text{est}}(t)}
$$

where $\mathbf s^t_{x}(i)$ is the activity at dipole $i$ and time $t$, and $\sigma_{x}(t)$ is the standard deviation of map $x$ at time $t$.

### Localization Accuracy {#sec-metric-loc}

Source onset was defined relative to the spike's rising phase, balancing a low probability of already-started propagation (favoring onset) against adequate SNR (favoring the peak, by which the source has typically spread). For both the simulation and resection cohorts, we used the 25% rising phase point (quarter rising phase, qrp) [@vorderwulbecke_high-density_2020]. For both cohorts, we computed the Euclidean distance from the location of maximal source activity to the target mask boundary (the true seed region for simulation, the resection volume for the resection cohort) — following @wang_geometry_2026 with distance 0 mm if that location already lies inside the mask.

### Source-to-iEEG Projection {#sec-virtual-ieeg}

For the simultaneous EEG/iEEG cohort (Clinical Dataset B), reconstructed cortical activity was projected onto the intracranial electrode coordinates as "virtual" iEEG, following @grova_intracranial_2016 using an infinite homogeneous conduction model with tissue conductivity set to 0.25 S/m (vs. the standard 0.33 S/m). Assuming 3 mm iEEG-MRI coregistration accuracy, the potential $\Phi$ at $r$ is stabilized against near-source instability with the same adjustment:

$$
\begin{align}\Phi(r) &= \frac{1}{4\pi \sigma} \sum_i \frac{\mathbf j_i \cdot(\mathbf r - \mathbf r_i)}{\lvert \mathbf r - \mathbf r_i\rvert^3} \text{ if } r>r_0 = 3 \text{ mm} \\ \Phi(r) &= \frac{1}{4\pi \sigma} \sum_i \frac{\mathbf j_i \cdot(\mathbf r - \mathbf r_0)}{\lvert \mathbf r - \mathbf r_i\rvert^3} \text{ if } r\le r_0 = 3 \text{ mm}\end{align}
$$

### Channel comparison {#sec-metric-channel}

We extracted a comparison window using an adaptive global field power threshold criterion rather than @grova_intracranial_2016's fixed-sample one (criterion in Annex). Within that window, the projected virtual iEEG activity (@sec-virtual-ieeg) was compared against ground-truth iEEG at each timepoint via polarity-invariant Pearson spatial correlation across channels ($|r|$, since the polarity of the iEEG is not clear), tracked over time. We additionally computed a win-rate for each other method against wCSET — the fraction of timepoints where wCSET is closer to ground truth — rather than a full all-against-all comparison.

### Statistical Analysis {#sec-stats}

Method comparisons are paired (by region for simulation, by subject for the resection cohort, by timepoint for the simultaneous EEG/iEEG cohort) and tested against a reference method, typically wCSET. Discrete outcomes (localization error) used the Wilcoxon signed-rank test (rank-biserial effect size); where the matched dimension carries serial or spatial correlation — Study 3's channel comparison (@sec-metric-channel) — we instead used a paired t-test with an autocorrelation-corrected effective sample size (Cohen's dz; full derivation in Annex). Continuous comparisons along a coordinate (SNR, time, perturbation severity) used cluster-based permutation testing (full procedure in Annex), with all p-values Benjamini-Hochberg FDR-corrected within their comparison family at α = 0.05.


# Results
```{python filename=plot_configuration.py}
COLORS = {
    "wcset":    "#2a78d6",  # blue
    "cset":     "#1baf7a",  # aqua
    "sloreta":  "#008300",  # green
    "dspm":     "#4a3aa7",  # violet
    "wmne":     "#e34948",  # red
    "beltrami": "#eb6834",  # orange - Study II/III only, see note below
}
LINE_COLOR = "#898781"  # muted ink - carries no

# transferred from processing_simf.qmd's comparison_plots.py - reimplemented
# with plain matplotlib (rather than MetricSuite.plot()'s seaborn FacetGrid)
# so it can use the same fixed method colors as the SPIKE resection figures;
# MetricSuite.plot()'s relational path has no way to pass a custom hue palette
# through to seaborn's FacetGrid.
# MCE excluded from every study: its L1 sparsity makes it react to
# correlation/AP-style metrics on a fundamentally different axis than the
# other five methods (near-zero spatial correlation whenever it's silent,
# but artificially clean precision-recall ranking whenever it fires) -
# not a meaningful signal about connectivity priors, just a metric artifact.
# Precision/AP figures also dropped from this document (Study 1 no longer
# plots precision_hrp/pp or ap_hrp/pp): the ground-truth "active" mask
# (gold > 0) they're scored against covers a huge, noise-independent
# fraction of cortex by hrp/pp (propagation has already spread that far),
# which sets a high, hard-to-move floor on AP - the metric doesn't track
# reconstruction quality the way correlation/localization error do, and no
# principled way was found to threshold the mask more strictly without
# picking an arbitrary, SNR-dependent "reconstructibility" cutoff.
# processing_simf.qmd still computes these metrics (for reference/appendix
# use), they're just not plotted here anymore.
METHODS = ["wcset", "cset", "sloreta", "dspm", "wmne"]
METHOD_LABELS = {
    "wcset": "wCSET", "cset": "CSET", "sloreta": "sLORETA", "dspm": "dSPM", "wmne": "wMNE",
    "beltrami": "Beltrami",
}
# beltrami is a 6th competitor computed only for the clinical cohorts (Studies
# II/III) - wCSET on the Laplace-Beltrami mesh eigenbasis, the GBF-like
# geometry-only baseline (see Section 2.3.3's surrogate-connectome
# construction). It has no counterpart in Study I's own METHODS, so it stays
# out of the METHODS list itself (which drives Study I's plots) and gets
# appended locally wherever Study II/III build their own method order.

# Formatting helpers for inline-quoted statistics throughout the Results and
# Discussion sections below - defined once here so every `{python} ...`
# inline reference downstream uses the same rounding/threshold convention,
# rather than re-implementing it at each of the many call sites. Numbers
# quoted in prose are pulled live from the same `stat.wilcoxon`/`.ttest_ess`/
# `.cluster_permutation` calls that build the figures (computed and
# cached once by each processing_*.qmd's Statistics section, reloaded here
# as an instant cache hit), rather than hand-typed, so that changing a test
# and re-rendering updates the prose automatically instead of silently
# drifting from what the code produces.
def fmt_p(p, thresh=0.001):
    """Bare comparison + value for prose, e.g. '< 0.001' or '= 0.023' - the
    prose supplies its own 'p'/'p_corrected' label immediately before the
    inline reference (e.g. `` p`{python} fmt_p(...)` `` renders 'p = 0.023'
    or 'p < 0.001'), since which label applies varies by context."""
    return f"< {thresh}" if p < thresh else f"= {p:.3f}"

# Reference-method annotation for the group_comparison/cluster_permutation
# figures below - neither mindmap function exposes a hook to customize its
# legend/tick-label text, so these mutate what's already drawn (in place, not
# replacing it) rather than reaching into the mindmap package itself.
def mark_reference(ax, reference, suffix=" (ref.)"):
    """Appends `suffix` to `reference`'s entry in `ax`'s already-built legend, in place."""
    for text in ax.get_legend().get_texts():
        if text.get_text() == reference:
            text.set_text(text.get_text() + suffix)
            break

def ref_labels(names, reference, suffix=" (ref.)"):
    """Tick-label list with `suffix` appended to `reference`'s entry."""
    return [f"{n}{suffix}" if n == reference else n for n in names]

def fmt_stat(value, digits=2):
    """Effect size (rank-biserial, Cohen's dz, etc.) for prose, e.g. '-0.48'."""
    return f"{value:.{digits}f}"

def fmt_num(value, digits=1):
    """Plain descriptive number (medians, mm, %, correlation units) for prose."""
    return f"{value:.{digits}f}"

def main_cluster(cluster_df):
    """The largest-mass cluster from a single competitor's
    `ClusterResult.clusters_by_pair[(reference, competitor)]` table -
    the one worth quoting in prose when a competitor has more than one
    (typically one real cluster plus a few negligible-mass leftovers)."""
    return cluster_df.loc[cluster_df["mass"].abs().idxmax()]

def competitor_row(result, competitor, reference="wcset"):
    """Row for one competitor from a `PairwiseResult.table` - the new API's
    table has arbitrary `group_a`/`group_b` columns instead of the old
    `"Label"` column, so this looks up whichever side of the pair
    `competitor` landed on."""
    t = result.table
    row = t[(t["group_a"] == reference) & (t["group_b"] == competitor)]
    if row.empty:
        row = t[(t["group_a"] == competitor) & (t["group_b"] == reference)]
    return row.iloc[0]
```

## Study I: Simulation-Based Validation {#sec-study1}

### Localization vs. Propagation {#sec-s1-localization}

```{python filename="simf_localization_stats.py"}
#| output: false
import mindmap as mm

simf_metrics = mm.metric.MetricSuite.load("./results/simf/flagship")
competitors = [m for m in METHODS if m != "wcset"]

# localization error at quarter-rising-phase only (see comparison.py in
# processing_simf.qmd): distance from each method's single loudest vertex to
# the true seed region, 0 mm if it lands inside it - one scalar per run, not
# a curve, so plotted as a box plot rather than a median+IQR band like the
# correlation figure below. `region` is registered alongside this metric
# (see comparison.py's `metrics.register(..., region=regions)`), so wCSET
# can be paired against every other method region-for-region (the reps
# within a region collapsed to one value first, by wilcoxon() itself)
# - a valid paired Wilcoxon signed-rank comparison - annotated directly on
# the box via `plot.group_comparison()`. `region`, not the finer-grained
# `run` this suite also carries, is the correct repeated-measures unit here:
# reps of the same region are correlated draws (same simulated source, only
# the noise differs), not independent trials - pairing by individual run
# would overstate n_pairs (pseudo-replication), same reasoning as the
# noise-sweep/degradation/surrogate cluster-permutation cells below.
# The `stat.wilcoxon` call below is identical to the one
# processing_simf.qmd's Statistics section already ran and cached, so this
# is an instant cache hit, not a recomputation.
loc1_results = simf_metrics.stat.wilcoxon(
    "localization_error", group_by="Method",
    comparisons=simf_metrics.stat.build_comparisons(["wcset"], competitors), pairing_col="region",
    filters={"phase": "qrp"},
)

# statistics quoted in the prose below, extracted from the same
# `loc1_results` table the box's own significance annotations come from.
def _loc1(method):
    return competitor_row(loc1_results, method)

loc1_sloreta_p = fmt_p(_loc1("sloreta")["p_corrected"], thresh=0.0001)
loc1_sloreta_r = fmt_stat(_loc1("sloreta")["effect_size"])
loc1_dspm_p = fmt_p(_loc1("dspm")["p_corrected"])
loc1_dspm_r = fmt_stat(_loc1("dspm")["effect_size"])
loc1_wmne_p = fmt_p(_loc1("wmne")["p_corrected"], thresh=0.0001)
loc1_wmne_r = fmt_stat(_loc1("wmne")["effect_size"])
loc1_cset_p = fmt_p(_loc1("cset")["p_corrected"])
loc1_cset_r = fmt_stat(_loc1("cset")["effect_size"])

# region-as-subject cluster-permutation summary vs. wCSET, over time - same
# design as the noise-sweep figures below (see
# mindmap/tutorials/analysis/metrics/metricsuite-noisesweep.ipynb), with
# `times` swapped in for `snr` as the swept coordinate. comparison.py
# registers `region` per (method, region) call on this metric. correlation
# is higher-is-better, and ascending time (not descending, unlike the SNR
# sweep) is the meaningful contiguity direction here. Identical call to the
# one already cached by processing_simf.qmd's Statistics section.
times_order = sorted(simf_metrics.to_df(metrics="correlation")["times"].unique())

corr1_results = simf_metrics.stat.cluster_permutation(
    "correlation", coord="times", group_by="Method",
    comparisons=simf_metrics.stat.build_comparisons(["wcset"], competitors), pairing_col="region",
    coord_order=times_order, higher_is_better=True,
    n_permutations=3000, seed=0,
)

# statistics quoted in the prose below: for each competitor, the single
# largest-mass cluster in its own cluster table (see `main_cluster` in
# plot_configuration.py above).
corr1_sloreta = main_cluster(corr1_results.clusters_by_pair[("wcset", "sloreta")])
corr1_dspm = main_cluster(corr1_results.clusters_by_pair[("wcset", "dspm")])
corr1_wmne = main_cluster(corr1_results.clusters_by_pair[("wcset", "wmne")])
corr1_cset = main_cluster(corr1_results.clusters_by_pair[("wcset", "cset")])

corr1_sloreta_p = fmt_p(corr1_sloreta["p_corrected"])
corr1_sloreta_dz = fmt_stat(corr1_sloreta["effect_size"])
corr1_dspm_p = fmt_p(corr1_dspm["p_corrected"])
corr1_dspm_dz = fmt_stat(corr1_dspm["effect_size"])
corr1_wmne_p = fmt_p(corr1_wmne["p_corrected"])
corr1_wmne_dz = fmt_stat(corr1_wmne["effect_size"])
corr1_cset_p = fmt_p(corr1_cset["p_corrected"])
corr1_cset_dz = fmt_stat(corr1_cset["effect_size"])
corr1_cset_start = fmt_num(corr1_cset["times_start"] * 1000, digits=0)
corr1_cset_end = fmt_num(corr1_cset["times_end"] * 1000, digits=0)

corr1_window_start = fmt_num(min(corr1_sloreta["times_start"], corr1_dspm["times_start"], corr1_wmne["times_start"]) * 1000, digits=0)
corr1_window_end = fmt_num(max(corr1_sloreta["times_end"], corr1_dspm["times_end"], corr1_wmne["times_end"]) * 1000, digits=0)

# Where the median-correlation gap between the two connectivity-informed
# methods (wCSET, CSET) and the three standard methods (sLORETA, dSPM, wMNE)
# is largest - same region-collapsed median curve `plot.cluster_permutation()`
# itself draws (mean over reps within region, then median across regions),
# used only to locate (not test) the widest separation, quoted in the prose
# above.
corr_collapsed = simf_metrics.to_df(metrics="correlation").groupby(
    ["Method", "region", "times"], as_index=False,
)["Value"].mean()
corr_median_curve = corr_collapsed.groupby(["Method", "times"], as_index=False)["Value"].median()
corr_pivot = corr_median_curve.pivot(index="times", columns="Method", values="Value").sort_index()
corr_gap = corr_pivot[["wcset", "cset"]].mean(axis=1) - corr_pivot[["sloreta", "dspm", "wmne"]].mean(axis=1)
corr1_gap_peak_time = fmt_num(corr_gap.idxmax() * 1000, digits=0)
```

We hypothesized that connectivity-informed methods would match standard methods at localizing a source's onset, while substantially outperforming them at tracking its subsequent propagation. We tested this using the simulation described in @sec-data-synthetic, which produces complex, fully known ground-truth activity from a single known source (@fig-flagship-example). At the quarter rising phase (@sec-metric-loc), wCSET's localization error differed significantly from every other method (@fig-localization-qrp; Wilcoxon signed-rank vs. wCSET, region-paired, FDR-corrected), but only modestly higher than CSET's (r = `{python} loc1_cset_r`) and dSPM's (r = `{python} loc1_dspm_r`), and substantially lower than sLORETA's (r = `{python} loc1_sloreta_r`) and wMNE's (r = `{python} loc1_wmne_r`).

As the source propagated beyond onset, wCSET's advantage emerged: spatial correlation with the ground truth, tracked from the quarter rising phase through the peak (@fig-correlation-time), was significantly higher for wCSET than every competitor's across nearly the entire displayed window (cluster-based permutation testing, region-paired, FDR-corrected), with much larger effect sizes against the three standard methods (Cohen's dz = `{python} corr1_sloreta_dz` for sLORETA) than against CSET (dz = `{python} corr1_cset_dz`), and the gap between connectivity-informed and standard methods widening toward the peak.

```{python filename="simf_correlation_plot.py"}
# median quarter-rising-phase / peak time of the simulated sensor EEG, pooled
# across all runs - median again (not mean), since the same per-run spread

# reference lines below, not quoted in the prose above.
qrp_median = simf_metrics.metadata["derived"]["qrp_time_median"]
pp_median = simf_metrics.metadata["derived"]["pp_time_median"]

corr1_fig, corr1_ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 5))
corr1_fig, corr1_ax = simf_metrics.plot.cluster_permutation(
```

### Robustness to Data Noise {#sec-s1-data-noise}

Sweeping simulated target SNR from 20 down to 1 (@sec-data-synthetic), localization error rose for every method as SNR decreased, but wMNE degraded much earlier than the rest — the other four methods stayed low until roughly SNR=4–5 before climbing (Annex Figure 4). wCSET's spatial-correlation advantage over every competitor, found above at fixed noise (@sec-s1-localization), held across nearly the full SNR range tested, down to SNR=1 (Annex Figure 5).

### Robustness to Prior Noise {#sec-s1-prior-noise}

```{python filename="simf_degradation_summary_stats.py"}
#| output: false
import mindmap as mm

deg_metrics_summary = mm.metric.MetricSuite.load("./results/simf/degradation")
_perm_d_summary = deg_metrics_summary.metadata["derived"]

# localization error (mm): wCSET's gradual rise vs. CSET's flat-then-sharp pattern
_loc_df_summary = deg_metrics_summary.to_df(metrics="localization_error", filters={"phase": "qrp"})
_loc_med_summary = _loc_df_summary.groupby(["Method", "percentage"])["Value"].median().unstack("percentage")

deg_summary_ref_loc_sloreta = fmt_num(_perm_d_summary["ref_loc"]["sloreta"])
deg_summary_loc_wcset_0 = fmt_num(_loc_med_summary.loc["wcset", 0])
deg_summary_loc_wcset_100 = fmt_num(_perm_d_summary["loc_wcset_100"])
deg_summary_loc_cset_lo_s = fmt_num(_loc_med_summary.loc["cset", 0:60].min())
deg_summary_loc_cset_hi_s = fmt_num(_loc_med_summary.loc["cset", 0:60].max())
deg_summary_loc_cset_100 = fmt_num(_loc_med_summary.loc["cset", 100])

# spatial correlation: wCSET's gradual decline vs. CSET's flat-then-sharp pattern
deg_summary_ref_corr_sloreta = fmt_num(_perm_d_summary["ref_corr"]["sloreta"], 2)
deg_summary_corr_wcset_0 = fmt_num(_perm_d_summary["corr_wcset_0"], 2)
deg_summary_corr_wcset_100 = fmt_num(_perm_d_summary["corr_wcset_100"], 2)
deg_summary_corr_cset_lo, deg_summary_corr_cset_hi = _perm_d_summary["corr_cset_0_60"]
deg_summary_corr_cset_lo_s = fmt_num(deg_summary_corr_cset_lo, 2)
deg_summary_corr_cset_hi_s = fmt_num(deg_summary_corr_cset_hi, 2)
deg_summary_corr_cset_100 = fmt_num(_perm_d_summary["corr_cset_100"], 2)
```

Using the connectome-perturbation procedure of @sec-connectome, we re-evaluated localization error and spatial correlation for CSET and wCSET, benchmarked against connectome-agnostic sLORETA. For localization error (Annex Figure 6), wCSET's error rose gradually across the full permutation range (`{python} deg_summary_loc_wcset_0`–`{python} deg_summary_loc_wcset_100` mm from 0% to 100%), while CSET's stayed comparatively flat through 60% (`{python} deg_summary_loc_cset_lo_s`–`{python} deg_summary_loc_cset_hi_s` mm) before rising sharply thereafter (`{python} deg_summary_loc_cset_100` mm at 100%). Statistically, CSET's early advantage over sLORETA reversed into a significant deficit once degradation passed that point; wCSET's own error, by contrast, started well below sLORETA's undegraded reference (`{python} deg_summary_ref_loc_sloreta` mm) and only grew worse than it late in the degradation range, never by a statistically significant margin.

For spatial correlation (Annex Figure 7), the same pattern held: wCSET's correlation with the ground truth declined gradually across the full range (`{python} deg_summary_corr_wcset_0`–`{python} deg_summary_corr_wcset_100` from 0% to 100%), while CSET's stayed relatively high through 60% (`{python} deg_summary_corr_cset_lo_s`–`{python} deg_summary_corr_cset_hi_s`) before dropping sharply by full permutation (`{python} deg_summary_corr_cset_100`). CSET's early advantage over sLORETA again reversed into a significant deficit at higher degradation; wCSET's correlation, meanwhile, closely approached sLORETA's own reference (`{python} deg_summary_ref_corr_sloreta`) by full permutation, without that difference reaching significance.


### Surrogate alternatives {#sec-s1-surrogates}
```{python filename="simf_surrogate_stats.py"}
#| output: false
import mindmap as mm

# beltrami replaced atlas-a2a/atlas-a2a-bin as of surrogate_reconstruction.py's
# latest run (see processing_simf.qmd) - kept in sync with the actual
# on-disk surrogate set, not the earlier atlas-a2a/-bin pair.
surrogates = ["beltrami", "fused", "fused-bin", "geom-atlas", "geom-atlas-bin"]
conditions = ["original"] + surrogates

# Reader-facing surrogate names differ from the on-disk `Surrogate` tags
# above - "fused" undersold the atlas provenance, and "geom-atlas" wrongly
# implied a population atlas (it's built purely from the subject's own
# mesh geometry) while also colliding with "geometry-only" language used
# elsewhere for the unrelated Beltrami-operator approach (Section 2.3.3).
# Data lookups/palette keys elsewhere still key off the original tags;
# only prose/inline-stat/axis text goes through this map.
SURROGATE_LABELS = {
    "fused": "atlas", "fused-bin": "atlas-bin",
    "geom-atlas": "local", "geom-atlas-bin": "local-bin",
}
methods = ["cset", "wcset"]

# Question of interest: does substituting a surrogate connectome change THIS
# method's own accuracy relative to using the real (original) connectome? -
# not whether cset differs from wcset (that's answered above, in
# simf_localization_error.py). One combined suite (original + every
# surrogate, tagged by `Surrogate`) is now built and saved by
# processing_simf.qmd's Statistics section - loaded here directly, never
# constructed ad-hoc; each panel below just filters it by `Method`/`phase`.
surr_metrics = mm.metric.MetricSuite.load("./results/simf/surrogates")
surr_comparisons = surr_metrics.stat.build_comparisons(["original"], surrogates)

# identical calls to the ones already cached by processing_simf.qmd's
# Statistics section. phase="qrp" always (no pp counterpart exists for
# this metric).
surr_loc_results = {}
for method in methods:
    surr_loc_results[method] = surr_metrics.stat.wilcoxon(
        "localization_error", group_by="Surrogate",
        comparisons=surr_comparisons, pairing_col="region",
        filters={"Method": method, "phase": "qrp"},
    )

# statistics quoted in the prose below.
def _loc_row(method, surrogate):
    return competitor_row(surr_loc_results[method], surrogate, reference="original")

loc_wcset_p = {s: fmt_p(_loc_row("wcset", s)["p_corrected"]) for s in surrogates}
loc_wcset_r = {s: fmt_stat(_loc_row("wcset", s)["effect_size"]) for s in surrogates}
_loc_wcset_r_abs = {s: abs(_loc_row("wcset", s)["effect_size"]) for s in surrogates}
loc_wcset_r_lo = fmt_stat(min(_loc_wcset_r_abs.values()))
loc_wcset_r_hi = fmt_stat(max(_loc_wcset_r_abs.values()))

# Correlation: same "original vs. surrogate" pattern, filtering the same
# combined suite by (method, phase) per panel instead of loading a separate
# pre-built suite.
surr_ref_corr = surr_metrics.metadata["derived"]["ref_corr"]

# identical calls to the ones already cached by processing_simf.qmd's
# Statistics section.
surr_corr_results = {}
for phase in ["qrp", "pp"]:
    for method in methods:
        surr_corr_results[(method, phase)] = surr_metrics.stat.wilcoxon(
            "correlation", group_by="Surrogate",
            comparisons=surr_comparisons, pairing_col="region",
            filters={"Method": method, "phase": phase},
        )

# statistics quoted in the prose below.
def _corr_row(method, phase, surrogate):
    return competitor_row(surr_corr_results[(method, phase)], surrogate, reference="original")

corr_wcset_beltrami_qrp, corr_wcset_beltrami_pp = _corr_row("wcset", "qrp", "beltrami"), _corr_row("wcset", "pp", "beltrami")
corr_wcset_beltrami_r_lo = fmt_stat(min(abs(corr_wcset_beltrami_qrp["effect_size"]), abs(corr_wcset_beltrami_pp["effect_size"])))
corr_wcset_beltrami_r_hi = fmt_stat(max(abs(corr_wcset_beltrami_qrp["effect_size"]), abs(corr_wcset_beltrami_pp["effect_size"])))

corr_wcset_beltrami_qrp_median = fmt_num(surr_metrics.metadata["derived"]["wcset_beltrami_qrp_median"], 2)
corr_wcset_beltrami_pp_median = fmt_num(surr_metrics.metadata["derived"]["wcset_beltrami_pp_median"], 2)
corr_dspm_qrp_ref = fmt_num(surr_ref_corr["qrp"]["dspm"], 2)
corr_dspm_pp_ref = fmt_num(surr_ref_corr["pp"]["dspm"], 2)
corr_sloreta_qrp_ref = fmt_num(surr_ref_corr["qrp"]["sloreta"], 2)
corr_sloreta_pp_ref = fmt_num(surr_ref_corr["pp"]["sloreta"], 2)

corr_wcset_fused_qrp, corr_wcset_fused_pp = _corr_row("wcset", "qrp", "fused"), _corr_row("wcset", "pp", "fused")
corr_wcset_fused_p_qrp, corr_wcset_fused_p_pp = fmt_p(corr_wcset_fused_qrp["p_corrected"]), fmt_p(corr_wcset_fused_pp["p_corrected"])
corr_wcset_fusedbin_qrp, corr_wcset_fusedbin_pp = _corr_row("wcset", "qrp", "fused-bin"), _corr_row("wcset", "pp", "fused-bin")
corr_wcset_fusedbin_p_qrp, corr_wcset_fusedbin_p_pp = fmt_p(corr_wcset_fusedbin_qrp["p_corrected"]), fmt_p(corr_wcset_fusedbin_pp["p_corrected"])
corr_wcset_geom_qrp, corr_wcset_geombin_qrp = _corr_row("wcset", "qrp", "geom-atlas"), _corr_row("wcset", "qrp", "geom-atlas-bin")
corr_wcset_geom_p_qrp = fmt_p(max(corr_wcset_geom_qrp["p_corrected"], corr_wcset_geombin_qrp["p_corrected"]))
corr_wcset_geom_pp, corr_wcset_geombin_pp = _corr_row("wcset", "pp", "geom-atlas"), _corr_row("wcset", "pp", "geom-atlas-bin")
corr_wcset_geom_p_pp = fmt_p(corr_wcset_geom_pp["p_corrected"])
corr_wcset_geombin_p_pp = fmt_p(corr_wcset_geombin_pp["p_corrected"])

# min/max |effect size| across all five surrogates, per phase - quoted in
# the prose below to back up the "small... to substantial" qualitative claim.
_corr_wcset_qrp_abs = [
    abs(corr_wcset_beltrami_qrp["effect_size"]), abs(corr_wcset_fused_qrp["effect_size"]),
    abs(corr_wcset_fusedbin_qrp["effect_size"]), abs(corr_wcset_geom_qrp["effect_size"]),
    abs(corr_wcset_geombin_qrp["effect_size"]),
]
corr_wcset_r_lo_qrp = fmt_stat(min(_corr_wcset_qrp_abs))
corr_wcset_r_hi_qrp = fmt_stat(max(_corr_wcset_qrp_abs))

_corr_wcset_pp_abs = [
    abs(corr_wcset_beltrami_pp["effect_size"]), abs(corr_wcset_fused_pp["effect_size"]),
    abs(corr_wcset_fusedbin_pp["effect_size"]), abs(corr_wcset_geom_pp["effect_size"]),
    abs(corr_wcset_geombin_pp["effect_size"]),
]
corr_wcset_r_lo_pp = fmt_stat(min(_corr_wcset_pp_abs))
corr_wcset_r_hi_pp = fmt_stat(max(_corr_wcset_pp_abs))
```

Using the dMRI-free connectome surrogates of @sec-connectome, we tested whether they could replace the true connectome without harming CSET/wCSET's accuracy (@fig-surrogate).

For localization error, wCSET was significantly *more* accurate using every surrogate than the true connectome, with small-to-moderate effect sizes (r = `{python} loc_wcset_r_lo`–`{python} loc_wcset_r_hi`) and no surrogate meaningfully better than the others (paired Wilcoxon vs. original connectome, region-paired, all five significant: p_corrected < 0.05). CSET showed the opposite sensitivity: beltrami and the local surrogate produced significant deficits, while the remaining three surrogates did not differ from the true connectome (full CSET breakdown in Annex Figure 8).

Spatial correlation showed the same pattern: every surrogate significantly *increased* wCSET's correlation with the ground truth relative to the original connectome at the peak, and four of five did so at the quarter rising phase (fused-bin fell short of significance there, p_corrected `{python} corr_wcset_fusedbin_p_qrp`) — growing from small effect sizes at the quarter rising phase (r = `{python} corr_wcset_r_lo_qrp`–`{python} corr_wcset_r_hi_qrp`) to substantial by the peak (r = `{python} corr_wcset_r_lo_pp`–`{python} corr_wcset_r_hi_pp`), with no surrogate meaningfully better than the others, and every surrogate's correlation remaining roughly 3–4× higher than dSPM's or sLORETA's own correlation with the true connectome. CSET showed the opposite pattern, generally significantly *lower* than the original connectome — consistently so for the atlas and both local surrogates (binarized and not) at both phases, and for the binarized atlas surrogate at the peak (but not at the quarter rising phase, where it fell short of significance), while never significantly different for beltrami (full CSET breakdown in Annex Figure 8).

```{python filename="simf_surrogate_plot.py"}

(a) Localization error (mm) at the quarter rising phase. (b, c) Spatial correlation with ground truth at the quarter rising phase (b) and peak phase (c). Dashed lines mark dSPM's and sLORETA's true-connectome medians as reference. Stars mark significance vs. the original (true) connectome (Wilcoxon signed-rank, region-paired, FDR-corrected). CSET's equivalent comparisons are reported in Annex Figure 8."

panel_letters = {"loc": "a", "qrp": "b", "pp": "c"}

# wCSET only in the main text - CSET's equivalent panels are qualitatively

surr_fig, surr_axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(len(conditions) * 1.3 * 2.4, 5.5))

# panel a: localization error at qrp.
```

## Study II: Clinical Localization (Resection Cohort) {#sec-study2}

### Localization Error {#sec-s2-localization}

```{python filename="results_resection_localization.py"}
#| output: false
import mindmap as mm

# METHODS/COLORS reused from plot_configuration.py above (same values) -
# MCE excluded from every study, see that cell's note. beltrami is added
# locally as a 6th method (RESECTION_METHODS) since it's only computed for
# the clinical cohorts, not Study I's simulation - see plot_configuration.py's
# note on METHOD_LABELS.
RESECTION_METHODS = METHODS + ["beltrami"]

# one MetricSuite for the whole cohort, built and stats-cached by
# processing_spike.qmd (resection_evaluation_metrics.py/spike_statistics.py)
# - loaded here directly, never built from a raw CSV.
resection_metrics = mm.metric.MetricSuite.load("./results/spike/resection")

# Excluded regardless of ILAE outcome - see processing_spike.qmd's Cohort
# Summary for the full breakdown (pat01: no usable resection mask AND no EEG
# channel locations; pat18: no real resection zone at all). Reproduced here
# (rather than read off the suite) so this cell's stat.wilcoxon() call below
# is byte-identical to the one processing_spike.qmd's spike_statistics.py
# already cached - without this, the call differs in its filters and silently
# recomputes over the wrong subject population instead of hitting the cache.
EXCLUDED_SUBJECTS = ["pat01", "pat18"]
all_subjects = resection_metrics.to_df(metrics="peak_distance_mm")["Subject"].unique()
included_subjects = [s for s in all_subjects if s not in EXCLUDED_SUBJECTS]

# seizure-free (ILAE=1) subjects, minus the exclusions above, quarter rising
# phase (the primary evaluation point, matching Study I's simulation cohort
# convention) - per explicit instruction, no longer faceted across every
# surgical outcome level. The suite-native replacement for a manual
# df[(df["ILAE"]==1) & ~df["Subject"].isin(EXCLUDED_SUBJECTS)] filter.
FILTERS = {"phase": "qrp", "ILAE": 1, "Subject": included_subjects}
resection_n = resection_metrics.metadata["derived"]["resection_n"]

competitors = [m for m in RESECTION_METHODS if m != "wcset"]

# box + raw per-subject points (no connecting lines) + Wilcoxon
# significance stars vs. wCSET, paired by subject, FDR-corrected.
# Identical call to the one already cached by processing_spike.qmd's
# Statistics section.
resection_results = {}
resection_results["peak_distance_mm"] = resection_metrics.stat.wilcoxon(
    "peak_distance_mm", group_by="Method",
    comparisons=resection_metrics.stat.build_comparisons(["wcset"], competitors),
    pairing_col="Subject", filters=FILTERS,
)

# statistics quoted in the prose below.
_peak = resection_results["peak_distance_mm"]

_peak_medians = resection_metrics.metadata["derived"]["peak_median"]

resection_peak_median_wcset = fmt_num(_peak_medians["wcset"])
resection_peak_median_cset = fmt_num(_peak_medians["cset"])
resection_peak_median_sloreta = fmt_num(_peak_medians["sloreta"])
resection_peak_median_dspm = fmt_num(_peak_medians["dspm"])
resection_peak_median_wmne = fmt_num(_peak_medians["wmne"])
resection_peak_median_beltrami = fmt_num(_peak_medians["beltrami"])

resection_peak_p_cset = fmt_p(competitor_row(_peak, "cset")["p_corrected"])
resection_peak_r_cset = fmt_stat(competitor_row(_peak, "cset")["effect_size"])
resection_peak_p_dspm = fmt_p(competitor_row(_peak, "dspm")["p_corrected"])
resection_peak_r_dspm = fmt_stat(competitor_row(_peak, "dspm")["effect_size"])
resection_peak_p_sloreta = fmt_p(competitor_row(_peak, "sloreta")["p_corrected"])
resection_peak_r_sloreta = fmt_stat(competitor_row(_peak, "sloreta")["effect_size"])
resection_peak_p_wmne = fmt_p(competitor_row(_peak, "wmne")["p_corrected"])
resection_peak_r_wmne = fmt_stat(competitor_row(_peak, "wmne")["effect_size"])
resection_peak_p_beltrami = fmt_p(competitor_row(_peak, "beltrami")["p_corrected"])
resection_peak_r_beltrami = fmt_stat(competitor_row(_peak, "beltrami")["effect_size"])

# smallest (i.e. closest-to-significant) corrected p-value among the four
# peak-distance comparisons that don't reach significance (all but wmne,
# see prose below) - quoted since no single one of those four is the
# natural one to single out.
_non_sig_competitors = [c for c in competitors if c != "wmne"]
resection_peak_p_min = fmt_p(min(competitor_row(_peak, c)["p_corrected"] for c in _non_sig_competitors))
```

Simulation offers a controlled testbed, but real clinical data will always differ. We evaluated localization accuracy against the resected epileptogenic zone in seizure-free patients (ILAE 1, n=`{python} resection_n`), alongside wMNE, sLORETA, dSPM, and the Beltrami-eigenbasis GBF variant (@sec-inverse) as a sixth competitor.

Peak-to-resection distance was lowest for wCSET (@fig-resection-localization; median `{python} resection_peak_median_wcset` mm), narrowly ahead of Beltrami (`{python} resection_peak_median_beltrami` mm) and sLORETA (`{python} resection_peak_median_sloreta` mm), then CSET (`{python} resection_peak_median_cset` mm), with dSPM (`{python} resection_peak_median_dspm` mm) and wMNE (`{python} resection_peak_median_wmne` mm) clearly worse. Of the five paired comparisons against wCSET (Wilcoxon signed-rank, subject-paired, FDR-corrected), only wMNE reached significance (p_corrected `{python} resection_peak_p_wmne`, r = `{python} resection_peak_r_wmne`); the rest did not, the closest being dSPM (p_corrected `{python} resection_peak_p_min`).

wCSET thus matched or exceeded every competitor's localization accuracy in real, noisier clinical data, reaching significance specifically against wMNE. This shows wCSET's propagation-tracking advantage from Study I does not come at the cost of localization accuracy.

## Study III: Clinical Dynamics (Simultaneous iEEG/EEG) {#sec-study3}

### Spatial Correlation Analysis

As the simulation suggested, source localization in the clinical resection cohort of Study II (@sec-s2-localization) yielded similar performance across methods; since connectivity-informed methods are designed to capture distributed activity rather than a single focal source, we now instead test whether they better reproduce the overall pattern of activity.

wCSET was compared against every competitor at the timepoint level (spatial correlation), via the autocorrelation-corrected paired test of @sec-stats.

```{python filename="results_intra_vieeg_significance.py"}
#| output: false
import mindmap as mm

# reuses METHODS/COLORS already defined above in plot_configuration.py, so
# method colors stay consistent with every other figure in this document.
# beltrami (6th competitor, clinical-only, see plot_configuration.py's note)
# is added to COMPETITORS below in processing_intra.qmd's own method order
# (["wcset", "sloreta", "cset", "dspm", "wmne", "beltrami"]) rather than
# appended after METHODS's order, so this cell's stat.ttest_ess() calls stay
# an exact, byte-identical match to the ones already cached by that file's
# Statistics section.

# combined suite (every sub-*/ subfolder concatenated) built and stats-cached
# by processing_intra.qmd's Statistics section - loaded here directly, never
# combined via concat() in this document.
vieeg_metrics = mm.metric.MetricSuite.load("./results/intra/combined")

# Only 4 subjects total (fixed), and 2 of them (12, 50) have deep sources with
# no visible spike on scalp EEG -- their EEG-derived source reconstruction
# (and therefore virtual iEEG) starts from an inherently less reliable signal
# than 34/48's. Stats are still computed for all 4 (SUBJECT_ORDER) - reused
# by the Annex - but the main-text figure below only plots
# MAIN_SUBJECTS (34/48); 12/50 are reported in the Annex
# instead (see prose above).
SUBJECT_ORDER = ["34", "48", "12", "50"]
MAIN_SUBJECTS = ["48", "34"]
SUBJECT_TITLES = {
    "34": "Subject 2",
    "48": "Subject 1",
    "12": "sub-12\n(no visible EEG spike)",
    "50": "sub-50\n(no visible EEG spike)",
}

# Only 4 subjects - too few for subject-level pairing (pairing_col="Subject"
# would treat n=4 as the sample size, no real power). Channels/timepoints
# within one subject are numerous but NOT independent (spatially/temporally
# correlated), so a plain Wilcoxon/t-test paired across them would overstate
# significance. Fix: an autocorrelation-corrected effective sample size
# (Thiebaux & Zwiers, 1984) in place of the raw channel/timepoint count -
# mindmap.core.stats.effective_sample_size, via
# suite.stat.ttest_ess(...) - see
# mindmap/tutorials/analysis/metrics/metricsuite-intra-vieeg.ipynb, which
# this cell adapts directly (measured lag-1 autocorrelation of the
# wCSET-competitor difference series on this exact data: 0.45-0.83 for
# timepoints, 0.16-0.52 for channels - large enough that the correction has
# real bite, not just a formality).
COMPETITORS = ["sloreta", "cset", "dspm", "wmne", "beltrami"]


def paired_diffs(subject, metric, coord):
    # exact post-dropna order already computed and cached by
    # processing_intra.qmd's Statistics section - reused verbatim both to
    # rebuild this diffs array and to keep the stat.ttest_ess() call
    # below (part of the cache key) an instant cache hit rather than a
    # silent recompute under a different order.
    order = vieeg_metrics.metadata["derived"]["subject_order"][subject][metric]
    df_sub = vieeg_metrics.to_df(metrics=metric, filters={"Subject": subject})
    wide = df_sub.pivot_table(index=coord, columns="Method", values="Value", aggfunc="mean").reindex(order)
    wide = wide.dropna(subset=["wcset"] + COMPETITORS)
    return {c: (wide["wcset"] - wide[c]).to_numpy() for c in COMPETITORS}, wide.index.tolist()


METRIC_BLOCKS = [
    ("correlation_spatial", "times", "Spatial corr.\n(diff per timepoint)"),
]

# statistics quoted in the prose below and drawn by the figure at the end of
# this section are collected into these two dicts, keyed by (subject,
# metric) - so the figure and the prose numbers come from exactly the same
# stat.ttest_ess() call, run once here.
vieeg_results = {}
vieeg_diffs = {}

for metric, coord, ylabel in METRIC_BLOCKS:
    for subject in SUBJECT_ORDER:
        diffs, order = paired_diffs(subject, metric, coord)
        # identical call to the one already cached by processing_intra.qmd's
        # Statistics section.
        vieeg_results[(subject, metric)] = vieeg_metrics.stat.ttest_ess(
            metric, group_by="Method", comparisons=vieeg_metrics.stat.build_comparisons(["wcset"], COMPETITORS),
            pairing_col=coord, subject_order=order, filters={"Subject": subject},
        )
        vieeg_diffs[(subject, metric)] = diffs

# statistics quoted in the prose below.
def _p(subject, metric, competitor):
    return competitor_row(vieeg_results[(subject, metric)], competitor)["p_corrected"]

def _neff(subject, metric, competitor):
    return competitor_row(vieeg_results[(subject, metric)], competitor)["n_eff"]

def _winrate(subject, metric, competitor):
    return vieeg_metrics.metadata["derived"]["win_rate"][f"{subject}|{metric}|{competitor}"]

def _dz(subject, metric, competitor):
    # ttest_ess's own effect size (Cohen's dz on the wcset-competitor
    # difference series) - positive means wCSET wins, matching the
    # win-rate/diff sign convention used elsewhere in this cell.
    return competitor_row(vieeg_results[(subject, metric)], competitor)["effect_size"]

vieeg_48_spatial_p_cset = fmt_p(_p("48", "correlation_spatial", "cset"))
vieeg_48_spatial_p_sloreta = fmt_p(_p("48", "correlation_spatial", "sloreta"))
vieeg_48_spatial_p_dspm = fmt_p(_p("48", "correlation_spatial", "dspm"))
vieeg_48_spatial_p_wmne = fmt_p(_p("48", "correlation_spatial", "wmne"))
vieeg_48_spatial_p_beltrami = fmt_p(_p("48", "correlation_spatial", "beltrami"))
vieeg_48_spatial_neff_cset = f"{_neff('48', 'correlation_spatial', 'cset'):.0f}"
vieeg_48_spatial_neff_sloreta = f"{_neff('48', 'correlation_spatial', 'sloreta'):.0f}"
vieeg_48_spatial_neff_dspm = f"{_neff('48', 'correlation_spatial', 'dspm'):.0f}"
vieeg_48_spatial_neff_wmne = f"{_neff('48', 'correlation_spatial', 'wmne'):.0f}"
vieeg_48_spatial_neff_beltrami = f"{_neff('48', 'correlation_spatial', 'beltrami'):.0f}"
vieeg_48_spatial_dz_cset = fmt_stat(_dz("48", "correlation_spatial", "cset"))
vieeg_48_spatial_dz_sloreta = fmt_stat(_dz("48", "correlation_spatial", "sloreta"))
vieeg_48_spatial_dz_dspm = fmt_stat(_dz("48", "correlation_spatial", "dspm"))
vieeg_48_spatial_dz_wmne = fmt_stat(_dz("48", "correlation_spatial", "wmne"))
vieeg_48_spatial_dz_beltrami = fmt_stat(_dz("48", "correlation_spatial", "beltrami"))

# min/max across the four uniform-direction competitors (cset/sloreta/dspm/wmne),
# for the compressed range quoted in prose - beltrami excluded (opposite direction).
_vieeg_48_spatial_dz4 = [_dz("48", "correlation_spatial", c) for c in ["cset", "sloreta", "dspm", "wmne"]]
vieeg_48_spatial_dz4_lo = fmt_stat(min(_vieeg_48_spatial_dz4))
vieeg_48_spatial_dz4_hi = fmt_stat(max(_vieeg_48_spatial_dz4))
_vieeg_48_spatial_neff4 = [_neff("48", "correlation_spatial", c) for c in ["cset", "sloreta", "dspm", "wmne"]]
vieeg_48_spatial_neff4_lo = f"{min(_vieeg_48_spatial_neff4):.0f}"
vieeg_48_spatial_neff4_hi = f"{max(_vieeg_48_spatial_neff4):.0f}"
_vieeg_48_spatial_p4 = [_p("48", "correlation_spatial", c) for c in ["cset", "sloreta", "dspm", "wmne"]]
vieeg_48_spatial_p4_max = fmt_p(max(_vieeg_48_spatial_p4))

# excludes beltrami deliberately: its raw per-timepoint win-rate sits below
# chance (unlike the other four), even though the autocorrelation-corrected
# paired test below does not find this difference significant - folding it
# into this range would make the "above chance" framing wrong either way.
# Reported separately in the prose instead.
_sub48_spatial_winrates = [_winrate("48", "correlation_spatial", c) for c in ["cset", "sloreta", "dspm", "wmne"]]
vieeg_48_winrate_min = f"{min(_sub48_spatial_winrates) * 100:.0f}"
vieeg_48_winrate_max = f"{max(_sub48_spatial_winrates) * 100:.0f}"
vieeg_48_winrate_pp_min = f"{(min(_sub48_spatial_winrates) - 0.5) * 100:.0f}"
vieeg_48_winrate_pp_max = f"{(max(_sub48_spatial_winrates) - 0.5) * 100:.0f}"
vieeg_48_beltrami_winrate = f"{_winrate('48', 'correlation_spatial', 'beltrami') * 100:.0f}"
```

Among the subjects with a visible EEG spike, the two responded very differently (@fig-intracranial-diff). Subject 1 showed the clearest advantage for wCSET: spatial correlation was significantly higher than sLORETA, dSPM, wMNE, and CSET alike, with wCSET winning `{python} vieeg_48_winrate_min`–`{python} vieeg_48_winrate_max`% of timepoints against these four competitors. Against Beltrami the pattern reversed but did not reach significance (p_corrected `{python} vieeg_48_spatial_p_beltrami`): wCSET won only `{python} vieeg_48_beltrami_winrate`% of individual timepoints, below the 50% chance level, but the difference was not statistically robust.

Subject 2 did not reproduce this pattern: wCSET's spatial correlation did not differ significantly from any competitor.


```{python filename="results_intra_vieeg_significance_plot.py"}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-intracranial-diff
#| fig-cap: "Per-timepoint spatial-correlation differences, wCSET minus each competitor, for the two subjects with a visible scalp EEG spike (sub-12/sub-50 are reported in the Annex). Win rate relative to the 50% chance line and effective sample size (n_eff) are annotated above each box. Stars mark significance from an autocorrelation-corrected paired t-test (ttest_ess)."
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt


def draw_diff_panel(ax, subject, metric, coord, title=None):
    diffs = vieeg_diffs[(subject, metric)]
    results = vieeg_results[(subject, metric)]

    data = [diffs[c] for c in COMPETITORS]
    bp = ax.boxplot(data, positions=range(len(COMPETITORS)), widths=0.5,
                     patch_artist=True, showfliers=False, zorder=2)
    for patch, c in zip(bp["boxes"], COMPETITORS):
        patch.set_facecolor(COLORS[c])
        patch.set_alpha(0.55)
    for element in ["whiskers", "caps", "medians"]:
        for line in bp[element]:
            line.set_color("#333333")

    rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
    for i, c in enumerate(COMPETITORS):
        y = diffs[c]
        x = i + rng.uniform(-0.15, 0.15, size=len(y))
        point_colors = np.where(y > 0, "tab:green", "tab:red")
        ax.scatter(x, y, s=6, alpha=0.45, c=point_colors, linewidths=0, zorder=3)

    ax.axhline(0, color="black", linewidth=1, linestyle="--", zorder=1)
    ax.set_xticks(range(len(COMPETITORS)))
    ax.set_xticklabels(COMPETITORS, fontsize=8)

    ymax, ymin = max(np.max(d) for d in data), min(np.min(d) for d in data)
    span = ymax - ymin
    for i, c in enumerate(COMPETITORS):
        row = competitor_row(results, c)
        # relative to the 50% chance line, not the raw win-rate - +17%/-13%
        # reads instantly (sign+color = direction, magnitude = how far from
        # a coin flip), where "37% vs. 67%" both need mentally subtracting
        # 50% first to compare. Read from processing_intra.qmd's precomputed
        # metadata["derived"], not recomputed here (a genuine derived stat).
        rel_win = vieeg_metrics.metadata["derived"]["win_rate"][f"{subject}|{metric}|{c}"] - 0.5
        p = row["p_corrected"]
        stars = "***" if p < 0.001 else "**" if p < 0.01 else "*" if p < 0.05 else "ns"
        win_color = "tab:green" if rel_win > 0 else "tab:red"
        ax.text(i, ymax + 0.10 * span, stars, ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=7, color="#222222")
        ax.text(i, ymax + 0.055 * span, f"{rel_win:+.0%}", ha="center", va="bottom",
                fontsize=7.5, color=win_color, fontweight="bold")
        ax.text(i, ymax + 0.01 * span, f"n_eff={row['n_eff']:.0f}", ha="center", va="bottom",
                fontsize=6, color="#666666")

    ax.set_ylim(ymin - 0.08 * span, ymax + 0.32 * span)
    if title:
        ax.set_title(title, fontsize=9)


# MAIN_SUBJECTS only (34/48) - sub-12/sub-50 (no visible EEG spike) are
# reported in the Annex instead (see prose above).
vieeg_fig, vieeg_axes = plt.subplots(
    len(METRIC_BLOCKS), len(MAIN_SUBJECTS),
    figsize=(4.2 * len(MAIN_SUBJECTS), 3.6 * len(METRIC_BLOCKS)),
    squeeze=False,
)

for row_i, (metric, coord, ylabel) in enumerate(METRIC_BLOCKS):
    for col_i, subject in enumerate(MAIN_SUBJECTS):
        ax = vieeg_axes[row_i, col_i]
        draw_diff_panel(ax, subject, metric, coord, title=SUBJECT_TITLES[subject] if row_i == 0 else None)
        if col_i == 0:
            ax.set_ylabel(ylabel, fontsize=8)

plt.tight_layout()
```

The spatial pattern behind these correlations is visible directly on the cortical surface (@fig-intra-reconstruction): wCSET's reconstruction stays more concentrated than sLORETA's in both subjects, at the timepoint where wCSET's own spatial correlation with the true intracranial recording peaks. The same fidelity shows up in the time domain (@fig-intra-channels): for each subject's single most temporally-correlated (and genuinely spike-containing, not spuriously correlated) intracranial channel, wCSET's virtual recording tracks the true channel's burst more closely than sLORETA's.
